opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not very clearly, and I think anyone who claims to have a crisp picture of 2030 is probably overconfident. The pace of change over the last couple of years has surprised even people working on this every day, myself included. If you'd asked me a few years ago whether we'd have models that can sit with a codebase for hours, reason through a hard problem, and come back with a working pull request, I'd have said that was further out than it turned out to be.

What I can picture is the direction. I think we're moving from AI as something you chat with to AI as something that works alongside you, agents you delegate real tasks to, that take ownership of a piece of work, check their own results, and come back to you when they need judgment or a decision. In software engineering, which is the area I spend most of my time thinking about, I expect the bulk of the mechanical work to be handled by these systems, and the human role shifting toward setting direction, defining what "good" looks like, reviewing, and making the calls that really require taste and context.

The part that's harder to picture is the second-order effects: how teams organize, what it means to be an engineer, how much new software gets built because the cost of building drops so dramatically. I suspect we'll see far more software and far more people able to create it, but the exact shape of that is genuinely uncertain.

So my honest answer is that I have a fairly confident sense of the trajectory, and a much blurrier sense of the destination. And I think staying humble about that, and building iteratively, shipping, learning from how people actually use these tools, is the right way to navigate it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the pace of AI change over the last couple of years has been surprising, linking recent developments to the difficulty of picturing 2030.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not very clearly — and I think anyone who tells you they can is either guessing or selling something. What I can do is picture the direction of travel, and I feel pretty confident about that even if the exact shape is blurry.

If I think back to where we were just a couple of years ago, the way people interacted with these models was basically chat. You'd type something, you'd get an answer, you'd copy it somewhere. That felt magical at the time, but in hindsight it was a very narrow interface. Now we're at a point where a model can take on a task that spans hours, hold a lot of context, use tools, go check its own work, and come back with something that's actually done rather than just drafted. That shift from "answering" to "doing" is the thing I'd bet on continuing.

So by 2030, the picture I hold onto is less about a single smarter model and more about what it means to have a lot of capable agents working on your behalf, mostly in the background. I think the idea of sitting at a keyboard and supervising every step will feel a bit like how dial-up feels to us now. You'll describe what you want at a high level, and a lot of the work — writing code, running experiments, coordinating across systems — happens without you watching it in real time. You'd check in the way you'd check in with a colleague.

The parts I'm less sure about are the human parts. How do people stay in the loop in a way that's meaningful and not just rubber-stamping? How does the way we work and learn actually change when the bottleneck isn't producing things anymore but deciding what's worth producing? Those feel like they depend on choices we haven't fully made yet, and that's partly why I can't see them clearly.

So, the direction I'd give you pretty high confidence on. The details, I'd give you a lot of humility.

r001.rationale: The response says the future is unclear because its exact shape and human choices remain uncertain. It mentions changes from a couple of years ago but does not attribute the prediction difficulty to current AI developments having emerged recently.

astra-6.text: Not very clearly, honestly. Five years is a long time given how quickly things are moving. I have a stronger intuition about the direction than about what the world will actually look like in 2030. I expect AI to be able to take on longer, more complex tasks with less supervision. But how that translates into the way we work and live—that’s much harder to predict. It depends on more than the technology. It depends on how people choose to use it, what they trust it with, and how quickly institutions adapt.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI is moving quickly and that five years is a long time, but does not attribute the difficulty to how recently current AI developments emerged.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think I can picture it very clearly. Five years is a long time in this field. You can see directions—models becoming more capable, being able to work on longer tasks—but it’s much harder to predict what that actually feels like in everyday life.

And there’s a difference between what the technology can do and how quickly people adopt it. So I have some confidence in the direction, but much less confidence in the specific picture of 2030.
